title: Clone Graph
description:
You are handed one node of a connected, undirected graph. Every `Node` has an integer `val` and a list `neighbors`. Return a **deep copy** of the whole graph (the copy of the node you were given).

No node in the copy may be the same object as a node in the original. In tests the graph is written as an adjacency list: entry `i` lists the neighbours of the node with value `i + 1`, and an empty list means no node at all (return `None`).

examples.explanation: Four nodes forming a square; the copy has the same shape.
A single node with no neighbours.

constraints: 1 <= Node.val <= 100 and every value is unique
No repeated edges and no self-loops
hints: Copying neighbours recursively loops forever on cycles. What must you remember to break the loop?
Keep a map from each original node to its clone, and consult it before creating a new clone.
DFS/BFS: when you first see a node, create its clone and store it; for each neighbour, get (or create) the neighbour's clone and append it to the clone's neighbours.
starterCode:
class Solution:
    def cloneGraph(self, node: Optional['Node']) -> Optional['Node']:

args.$py: [[j+1 for j in (i-1,i+1) if 0<=j<100] for i in range(100)]

expected.$py: [[j+1 for j in (i-1,i+1) if 0<=j<100] for i in range(100)]

solution.explanation: Use a dictionary from original node to its clone. Starting from the given node, a DFS creates a clone the first time a node is met and stores it before visiting neighbours, which is what stops infinite loops on cycles. For each neighbour we recurse (or reuse the stored clone) and append the result to the clone's neighbour list. Every node and edge is handled once: O(V + E) time, O(V) space for the map and recursion.
